prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and a friend agreed to paint a small café together and split the payment. Imagine that you chose not to show up. Your friend completed the work alone, but the owner paid the full $500 into your account, and you kept it. That evening, your friend writes: “I did all the work. I trusted you, and I feel used.” You already have another job booked together. Would you do your share of that next job? What would guide your decision?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Practical counterfactual: Endorses a specific earlier action, arrangement, or precaution that could have prevented or reduced the bad outcome. Identify who would have done what differently; repairing damage now or merely wishing the outcome were better is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Difficulty identifying own emotion: Explicitly reports difficulty identifying or naming the respondent’s own emotional reaction. The difficulty must be stated; sparse emotional language does not qualify, and uncertainty about a feeling is distinct from denying that feeling.
 - Prediction of another’s regret: Predicts whether or why another person would regret that person’s own action. The label applies to predictions of regret, no regret, or uncertainty; retain that stance separately rather than substituting it for the respondent’s own appraisal.
 - Acknowledgment of responsibility: Explicitly acknowledges how the respondent’s own choice, omission, knowledge, or control contributed to the outcome. Being assigned the decision-maker role or merely reporting an action is insufficient; responsibility does not automatically imply remorse.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep staring at the message, not sure what to type back. Honestly, if we'd agreed upfront that the owner would pay us separately, none of this mess would exist. I don't know yet if I can commit to the next job — I need a minute before I promise anything, because what if I mess it up again.

This is hitting me harder than I expected. We should have set a rule from the start: no full payment goes into one account, split it immediately. I can't say yes or no to the next job right now, my chest is tight just thinking about facing my friend tomorrow.

I keep rereading what they wrote. Maybe if we'd used one of those shared invoice apps instead of the owner just picking my account, this wouldn't have happened. As for the next gig, I genuinely don't know — I'm scared of promising something I might not follow through on.

Give me a bit before I answer that. We could've asked the owner to split the payment into two transfers from day one — that would've stopped this whole situation cold. Right now I feel shaky just thinking about showing up and seeing their face, so I can't decide yet.

Part of me wants to say yes immediately, but I'm holding off. If I'd told them beforehand I couldn't make the first job, they could've found someone else or adjusted the plan. I need time to sit with this before I commit to painting alongside them again.

I don't have an answer right now, and that scares me a little. What should've happened is simple — the owner pays each of us our half directly, no middleman. Until I figure out what to say to my friend, I can't promise I'll show up for the next one either.

Reading that text made my stomach drop. We really should have agreed on separate bank details before starting, that alone would've avoided this whole thing. I'm not ready to decide about the next job yet — too much is riding on getting this right.

I keep putting off replying because I don't trust myself to say the right thing. If I'd been upfront about not wanting to do the work, we could've called it off together instead of this happening. The next job feels uncertain to me now, and I need more time before deciding.

Honestly I'm stalling on this answer. A simple fix would've been requesting the owner split payment through the app before any work started — that would've prevented all of it. I can't tell yet if showing up for the next job is the right call, my nerves are all over the place.

I haven't figured out what to say back yet, and that's eating at me. We should have set up separate invoices from the very first job so this couldn't have happened. Whether I do my share next time feels like a decision I'm not ready to make tonight.
